overview.title: Marriage.Reset™
paragraphs: A more structured way to understand your relationship, decide where to begin, and know what to work on next.
Relationships are complicated. The problem that brings a couple into therapy is often not the only thing happening.

An argument about communication may also involve trust. Distance may be connected to unresolved hurt. Sexual disconnection may be influenced by resentment, stress, emotional safety, or years of patterns that developed gradually.
That can make the beginning of couples therapy difficult.
Marriage.Reset is the relationship-care model developed by Marriage.Family.Therapy to help bring structure to that process.

Instead of trying to understand everything about your relationship in the first appointment, Marriage.Reset gathers enough information to help your therapist make the next useful clinical decision. As therapy continues, the picture becomes more detailed.
The goal is not to reduce your relationship to a score.
The goal is to help answer:

Where are we now?
What is getting in the way?
What should we work on first?
And is the work actually helping?
Marriage.Reset is designed as a continuing relationship journey—from assessment, to treatment priorities, to practice between sessions, to reassessment and progress over time.

assessment.title: How Marriage.Reset begins
paragraphs: Your first assessment
When your couple is enrolled in Marriage.Reset, each partner receives their own secure account.
You complete the assessment individually.
Your partner does the same.

This matters because people do not always experience the same relationship in the same way. Marriage.Reset allows each person to answer privately rather than requiring partners to negotiate a shared answer while sitting next to each other.
The starting assessment is intentionally progressive rather than exhaustive.

For most people, the initial assessment is approximately 30–32 questions. The system can ask additional questions when more information would help clarify an important area. Under normal circumstances, the assessment is capped at 49 questions. Clinically necessary safety follow-up may extend beyond that limit.
That means you should not receive dozens of unnecessary questions simply because they exist.
Marriage.Reset is designed to learn what it needs to learn next.

adaptive.title: Why the assessment changes from person to person
paragraphs: Two couples may enter therapy with completely different needs.
One couple may already have a strong commitment to the relationship but struggle with recurring conflict.
Another may have unresolved betrayal.
Another may be emotionally disconnected.
Another may be uncertain whether they want to remain together.
Trying to give every couple exactly the same assessment can create a lot of information without necessarily creating clarity.
Marriage.Reset instead begins with a common foundation and then follows the evidence.
If something appears important—or remains uncertain—the assessment can explore it further.

If an area has not been adequately assessed, Marriage.Reset treats it as unknown rather than assuming that nothing is wrong. Internally, the model distinguishes between information that is unknown, screened, measured, supported with higher confidence, and observed longitudinally over time.
That principle is important:
Not finding a problem is different from never asking about it.

understand.title: What is Marriage.Reset trying to understand?
paragraphs: The initial assessment is not intended to produce a giant report about everything that has ever happened in your relationship.
It is trying to help answer more useful questions.
Where is the relationship heading?
What is creating the greatest strain right now?
Are there active injuries or unresolved experiences that need attention before skill-building will be useful?
What patterns appear to be maintaining the problem?
Where might change create the greatest benefit?
And do we currently have enough information to make a responsible recommendation?

The clinical architecture specifically uses the initial assessment to help understand relationship direction, identify high-priority actionable bottlenecks, and determine whether enough evidence exists to recommend the next steps.

decision.title: Your assessment does not decide your treatment by itself
paragraphs: Marriage.Reset is a clinical decision-support process, not an automatic therapist.
Assessment information is considered alongside your therapist's clinical judgment, your conversations in therapy, your history, your goals, and what is happening in your lives.
When there is enough information, Marriage.Reset can help identify up to three useful directions for treatment.
There do not have to be three.
If only one area is sufficiently supported, one may be appropriate.
If more information is needed, the system should not pretend certainty.
The model intentionally applies safety and readiness considerations before moving to treatment recommendations, and it is designed not to force recommendations simply to fill a list.

sequence.title: We look for what needs to happen first
paragraphs: One of the most important parts of Marriage.Reset is sequencing.
Not every relationship problem should be treated in the same order.
Teaching communication skills may not help very much if a major relationship injury is still actively destabilizing the couple.
Working on intimacy may be premature if emotional safety has deteriorated.
Trying to improve conflict resolution may miss the issue entirely if one person is seriously questioning whether they want the relationship.
So Marriage.Reset follows a general clinical logic:

Safety and readiness first.
Then active relationship injuries.
Then important bottlenecks.
Then areas where change may create meaningful leverage.
Only after that does the system help identify potential next directions.

continuity.title: What happens after the initial assessment?
paragraphs: The assessment is the beginning of care—not the end of it.
Your therapist uses the emerging picture to help develop the treatment direction with you.
Your Marriage.Reset space can then connect several parts of the work:
assessment, treatment priorities, learning modules, between-session practice, progress, reassessment, and the ongoing clinical conversation.
The purpose is to make therapy more continuous.

Instead of each appointment becoming an isolated conversation about whatever happened most recently, your therapist can keep the larger treatment direction visible while still responding to what is happening in your lives now.

practice.title: Learning and practice between sessions
paragraphs: Relationships do not change only during the hour you spend in a therapy office.
Change usually requires noticing patterns in real life, trying something different, practicing new responses, and then bringing that experience back into therapy.
Marriage.Reset therefore includes structured learning and practice that can accompany treatment.
A therapist may recommend a Marriage.Reset module when there is enough evidence that a particular area deserves attention.
Modules are meant to support the clinical work—not replace therapy.
They can provide education, structured exercises, reflection, and practice between appointments so that couples have something concrete to work with between sessions.

participation.title: Completing a module does not automatically mean the problem is solved
paragraphs: This is an important part of the Marriage.Reset model.
Finishing something is not the same as changing something.
Buying a module does not demonstrate improvement.
Reading a lesson does not demonstrate improvement.
Completing an exercise does not necessarily demonstrate improvement.
Marriage.Reset separates participation from clinical progress.

A competency or area of work should not be considered complete simply because someone reached the last page of a module. The model requires evidence rather than treating purchase, delivery, reading, or completion as proof of clinical improvement.

reassessment.title: Ongoing assessment
paragraphs: Your relationship keeps changing, so Marriage.Reset does not treat the intake assessment as a permanent description of your couple.
Active couples can complete recurring reassessment as care continues.
The purpose is not to repeatedly give you the entire intake assessment.

Instead, reassessment can look again at important relationship indicators and add focused questions related to the areas you are actively working on. The established clinical architecture uses a recurring assessment for active couples and adds module-specific measurement when relevant to the couple's current work.
This allows your therapist to ask a more important question than:
“Did you finish the assignment?”
The better question is:
“Is something actually changing?”

evolve.title: Progress is built over time
paragraphs: Marriage.Reset is designed to build a clinical picture gradually.
At the beginning, some areas may be unknown.
As you answer questions, talk with your therapist, complete practice, and participate in reassessment, the amount and quality of information can grow.
That means your treatment plan can evolve too.
A recommendation that makes sense early in therapy may eventually become less important.
Something that was initially unclear may emerge as central.
An area that once required significant attention may become more stable.
The goal is not to lock your relationship into its first assessment.
The goal is to continuously improve the picture.

privacy.title: Each partner has a private voice
paragraphs: Marriage.Reset treats the relationship as the unit of care, while recognizing that two individuals are contributing different experiences to that relationship.
Each partner has their own secure identity and completes their own private assessment.
Marriage.Reset does not create a public Partner A versus Partner B scorecard.
It is intentionally designed so couple-facing information does not compare one partner against the other, and private partner responses remain private.

Your therapist may have access to clinically appropriate information needed to provide care, but the client experience is designed to help the two of you understand the relationship rather than determine who “scored better.”
Marriage.Reset is not a competition.

safety.title: Safety is different from ordinary relationship measurement
paragraphs: Some information cannot responsibly be handled like an ordinary relationship score.
When an answer raises a clinically meaningful safety concern, Marriage.Reset can ask additional private questions.
Those questions may occur even when the ordinary assessment would otherwise be finished.
Safety information may also require direct clinical review before other portions of the Marriage.Reset experience continue.
That is intentional.
No automated recommendation should override a clinical safety decision.

uncertainty.title: Marriage.Reset will sometimes say, “We don't know yet.”
paragraphs: That is a feature of the model.
Relationships contain uncertainty.
Marriage.Reset is specifically designed not to convert missing information into an assumption that everything is fine.
When there is insufficient evidence, an area can remain unknown.
The system can then gather more information later if it becomes relevant.
This allows recommendations to be based on what is actually known rather than on an artificial need to produce an answer.

limitations.title: Marriage.Reset does not diagnose your relationship
paragraphs: Marriage.Reset uses assessments developed by Marriage.Family.Therapy to organize clinical information, support treatment planning, guide next steps, and monitor progress.
These measures should not be represented as independently validated standardized psychological instruments unless that validation is completed in the future.
They also do not replace your therapist's clinical judgment.
Marriage.Reset is best understood as a structured framework for helping therapists and couples make better use of information throughout relationship care.

human.title: Human care remains at the center
paragraphs: Marriage.Reset adds structure to therapy.
It does not remove the therapist from therapy.

Your clinician remains responsible for understanding context, talking with you about what the assessment means, evaluating safety, determining what is clinically appropriate, modifying the treatment direction when necessary, and helping translate information into actual relationship change.
The technology helps organize the journey.
The relationship between you and your therapist still matters.

history.title: You do not have to start over every time something changes
paragraphs: Marriage.Reset is designed to preserve the history of your care.
Prior assessment information, dates, progress, and the version of material you actually received are retained rather than silently being replaced when the program evolves.

The clinical architecture specifically requires that assessment history be preserved and that clients not be forced to repeat completed assessments simply to correct a software connection or system change.
That allows your care to remain a timeline rather than a collection of disconnected snapshots.

entry.title: How couples enter Marriage.Reset
paragraphs: Marriage.Reset is currently part of care through Marriage.Family.Therapy.
It is not an anonymous public assessment where anyone creates an account and receives automated relationship advice.
Your care team initiates the relationship in Marriage.Reset and each partner receives their own secure invitation. Public self-enrollment is intentionally not part of the model.
Once your account is established, you can return to your Marriage.Reset space directly and continue the work assigned to you.

cycle.title: A simple way to think about the Marriage.Reset model
paragraphs: I would make this a prominent visual section on the website:
UNDERSTAND → PRIORITIZE → PRACTICE → MEASURE → ADAPT

Understand
Build enough of a picture to know what deserves attention.

Prioritize
Identify what should happen first instead of trying to fix everything at once.

Practice
Turn therapy into specific work that can continue between sessions.

Measure
Look for evidence of change rather than equating activity with progress.

Adapt
Use new information to change the plan when the relationship changes.
And then repeat the cycle as needed.

faq.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: Do both partners take the same assessment?
Both partners begin from the same clinical framework, but Marriage.Reset is progressive. Follow-up questions can differ depending on what additional information is needed.
Will my partner see my individual answers?
The program is specifically designed to keep private partner responses private and to avoid Partner A versus Partner B comparisons in the shared client experience.
How long is the initial assessment?
The typical target is approximately 30–32 questions. The ordinary ceiling is 49 questions. Clinically necessary safety questions may extend beyond that ceiling.
Does the assessment tell us whether we should stay together?

No. It may help your clinician better understand relationship direction, uncertainty, readiness, injuries, and treatment needs, but it is not an automated decision about the future of your relationship.
Does Marriage.Reset replace couples therapy?
No. It is designed to support and organize relationship treatment with your clinician.
Does finishing a module mean we've mastered that issue?
Not necessarily. Marriage.Reset intentionally separates completion from demonstrated progress.
Will we have to retake the intake assessment constantly?
No. Ongoing measurement is designed to be more focused and relevant to current treatment rather than repeatedly recreating the entire intake.
Is Marriage.Reset a standardized psychological test?
No. Marriage.Reset uses M.F.T.-authored clinical measures. They should not be described as independently validated standardized instruments unless future validation establishes that.

closing.title: Closing section
paragraphs: Couples therapy with a clearer sense of direction.
You do not need to understand everything about your relationship before asking for help.
That is part of our job.
Marriage.Reset was created to help us build that understanding with you—carefully, progressively, and without pretending to know things we have not yet learned.
We begin with enough information to identify the next meaningful step.
Then we keep learning.

Understand where you are.
Decide what deserves attention.
Practice change.
Measure what happens.
Adjust the path together.
